a3_landing: Four hundred steps with lamps lit, and two landings on the way down. The wall carvings begin as proper mason's work and degrade, somewhere below the first landing, into gouges cut in a hurry by hands that were not dwarf hands and were not holding dwarf tools. On the second landing there is a shrine with nine niches cut into it at eye height.
a3_dark_descent: Four hundred steps in complete darkness with one hand on the wall, feeling the carvings change under the palm from proper tool-work into something scratched in a hurry. At the ninetieth step something comes up past the company on the outer edge of the stair, entirely unhurried, breathing on a count of nine. It does not touch anybody, and it does not stop counting, and it does not come back.
a3_scout_descent: The stair is roped and Kettle goes a full flight ahead of everybody, working on tugs: one for clear, two for wait where you are, three for come down after me. She gives one, and then another, and then a third, and then two in quick succession. After that the rope goes slack in your hands without any signal at all, and it stays slack.
a3_shrine: The stair-shrine holds nine niches, eight of them containing dwarf tokens gone black with age, and the ninth standing empty and warm enough to feel from a foot away. The lip of the shrine has been worn into a groove by something that has been set down there and taken back up a great many times.
a3_shrine_set: The ninth iron goes into the warm niche, which accepts it the way a lock accepts its own key. The entire hill goes quiet for the length of one breath. Then the count starts again somewhere below, slower than before, apparently satisfied, and entirely uninterested in anybody standing on the stair.
a3_lit: A lamp struck on the stair catches the thing on the outside of the flight for exactly one second: a Warden's cloak, a Warden's boots, and above the collar nothing that a helmet would ever fit. It continues upward past the company without turning, and its count does not falter.
a3_overtake: The slack rope leads down two flights to Kettle, who is flat against the wall with her own hand over her mouth, alive and extremely angry about it. She points down at the stairfoot, where a work-gang of Fenkin is carrying crates across the bottom of the stair in single file.
a3_stairfoot: The foot of the great stair is a crossing of ways in warm moving air. To the left a flooded gallery with lamplight lying on the water; ahead the pay-hall doors standing ajar; to the right a chapel light and, below that, the sound of a mill wheel turning. There is a breach in one wall where the vault cut into the old barrow, a cutting-shop with a cold forge beyond it, and at the far end of everything, a door.
a3_flood: The flooded gallery is chest-deep and as warm as bathwater, with lamplight further down it and a flat-bottomed ferry poling toward you. Three Fenkin are aboard, and a crate is lashed amidships. The crate is eighteen inches of dwarf oak, and it is not making crate noises.
a3_flood_swim: Sixty yards of warm black water with kit held above the head and the ferry's pole going past close enough to touch. Halfway across, something long turns over in the depth beneath the company, unhurried, indifferent, entirely uninterested in five people making a noise on the surface. It has the manner of an animal that has been extremely well fed for a considerable time.
a3_ledge: The maintenance ledge above the waterline is eleven inches wide, cut for dwarves without packs rather than men in mail. The ferry passes below close enough that you can hear the crate being spoken to, patiently, in a language that appears to consist entirely of numbers.
a3_ferry: Eleven seconds of violence in waist-deep water puts three Fenkin over the gunwale, and then there is nothing to do except look at the crate. Eighteen inches of dwarf oak, air holes bored through the lid in a ring of nine, and inside it something that has stopped making noise in order to listen to you.
a3_crate: The crate holds a Warden of the second relief patrol, alive, wrists bound in a knot Ilsabet recognises and will not name. He is blindfolded, and he is counting under his breath in a rhythm the company has now heard four times today and never once wanted to hear from a human throat.
a3_free: The lid comes off and the bound Warden inside is cut free and carried out between two of you, dead weight and still counting steadily. Nyre holds his head as they go and tells him, over and over, that the number is wrong. It is the only argument anybody has available down here, and he does not appear to hear it, but he does not stop being carried either.
a3_gangpass: Three Fenkin lamps held at Fenkin height, and the company poles a ferry down a flooded dwarf gallery in the middle of a work-file that never once looks up. You learn more in that quarter hour than in two days on the moor: what the crates are for, where they go, and how often they go there.
a3_payhall: The deep pay-hall is ankle-deep in water and echoes badly. A rack on the far wall holds eight key-irons in eight sockets with a ninth socket standing empty; the pay-bell waits on its stand beside it. The paymaster himself lies face down across his own table, and both his sleeves are empty from the elbow.
a3_paymaster: Turned over, the paymaster has no hands and no other injury anywhere on him. Inside his coat is a confession written in a hand that had to hold the pen in its teeth: that the ninth hand must be a hand that signs, that he signed for nine years, and that in the end he simply stopped.
a3_eight: Up close the rack is warm to the hand, and every one of the eight irons is seated in a socket that is warmer still than the iron. The ninth socket stands empty and worn bright around the mouth, as though something has been drawn out of it and put back a great many times. The whole rack is humming faintly, the way a bowstring hums in the moment before it is loosed.
a3_one_iron: One iron lifts out, and the rack's hum climbs a full tone as seven irons take up the load of the eighth's absence. Ilsabet says, quietly and with great precision, that the company now has about eleven minutes of the hill's patience remaining, and not one second longer than that.
a3_walltally: Behind the rack the wall carries a tally cut in groups of nine, going back nine hundred years in nine distinguishable hands, and then further back in a hand that is not dwarf work at all. In the final group, eight strokes have been cut cleanly and a ninth has been begun.
a3_chapel: The chapel of the Compact holds nine benches and a wall of tally, and at a clerk's writing desk in front of them a courteous grey man in a good coat stands up as the company comes in. He greets the Ninth Sword by name and by number, apologises for the temperature of the room, and offers the captain the only chair in it. Behind him, the tally-wall runs from floor to ceiling in groups of nine.
a3_terms3: Coren Vale explains the arithmetic the way a factor explains compound interest. The thing behind the door cannot be killed, and cannot be woken while the count holds. Eight irons hold the lid, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the frontier has been paying that instalment for nine hundred years without ever being told.
a3_offer: The offer is made plainly and without any threat in it at all. Vale is ninety-one years old and extremely tired, and the ninth hand's place falls vacant on his death. For one of the five, named by the captain today, he will hand over the iron, the ledger, the garrison's entire back pay, and nine more years of the frontier's peace.
a3_counter: The counter-offer is put to him straight: the company will close the door properly, all nine irons seated, with no hand at all keeping any count afterwards. Vale's face does something complicated and rather human. In ninety-one years nobody has proposed it to him, and he is not certain that it cannot be done.
a3_attack: Vale does not defend himself and does not appear to need to, because the chapel undertakes it on his behalf. Nine benches worth of accumulated dust stands up in the approximate shapes of the people who once sat on them. Dellach's first swing passes clean through a grey man's coat and strikes the writing desk standing behind it.
a3_kill_vale: Coren Vale dies at his own desk in about the time it takes to say a number aloud, and the count stops. Not slows: stops, everywhere in the hill at once. In the silence afterwards you can hear eight irons taking up a load that they were never designed to carry without a ninth.
a3_valebook: Vale's tally-book and the ninth hand's ring come off a dead man's desk together. The book runs to eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine different hands, the last of them his own. The ring is warm, and it is sized, unmistakably, for whichever hand picks it up next.
a3_wheel: The wheel-house under the pay-hall holds a dwarf pump the size of a barn, its wheel turning steadily in a race of black water. Three of its nine paddles have been hacked away and a Fenkin crew is working on the fourth with axes, without hurry, in the manner of men on a long contract.
a3_pump: A short brutal fight in a very loud room, and then an hour of carpentry: Dellach and Odd holding a paddle in place while Ilsabet lashes it. The water in the race drops a hand's width by the end of it, and the deep stays dry a while longer, for whatever that turns out to be worth.
a3_flood_deep: The wheel jams on a poleaxe haft and the race backs up within minutes, sending water the wrong way through nine hundred years of dwarf engineering. It goes down into the lower hall, where the crates are stacked in rows, and where the work-file is still working and has not been warned.
a3_race: The wheel-race is crossed on the axle housing with the wheel turning a foot behind your head, nine paddles coming round in an order you can learn if you watch for long enough. The gap between two paddles is exactly as wide as one man who does not hesitate in the middle of it.
a3_barrow: The breach in the vault wall opens into the barrow the dwarves cut through and believed they had merely cut through. It is a king's chamber with nine attendants seated around a king who is not present. Their plaques are still perfectly legible, and every one of the nine hands is pointing the same way.
a3_plaques: The nine plaques read in order, and they are not names at all but offices: the one who counts, the one who carries, the one who signs, and onward to the ninth, which is the one who is owed. All nine of the stone hands are pointing at the chamber's inner door.
a3_close: Two hours of rubble, mortar dust, and Dellach's shoulder against a slab that does not want to move, and the breach is closed about as well as five people can close it. Everybody understands, without any need to discuss the matter, that this is housekeeping rather than a solution. It will hold for exactly as long as nothing on the other side of it minds being shut in.
a3_through: The way through the barrow's inner chamber to the door gallery passes nine empty attendant chairs and one that is occupied. Whatever is sitting in it has been sitting there since before the dwarves cut their first gallery into this hill, and it does not turn its head as the company files past.
a3_forge: The cutting-shop is where the irons were made: a cold forge, a tally-die still bolted to its anvil, racks of blanks gone entirely to rust. The cutting-orders remain pinned to the bench under a stone. A dwarf smith is folded up beneath the bellows with his tools laid out beside him in careful order.
a3_cut: Three hours of cold work on a die that badly wants a striker and a proper smith, with Ilsabet reading the tally-order aloud stroke by stroke while Dellach swings. What comes off the anvil at the end of it is a ninth key-iron that is nine parts correct and one part entirely yours.
a3_die: The tally-die comes off the anvil in eleven minutes of work and wraps into forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what any key-iron says. Ilsabet observes, while lashing it into her pack, that this makes it either the most valuable object in the hill or the most dangerous one. She then observes that it is quite obviously both at once, and stops talking about it.
a3_orders: The cutting-orders read like any legion requisition until the final clause. Nine irons commissioned at the founding, eight to be cut with the holding tally, and the ninth to be cut with a name left deliberately blank, to be filled in by the hand that would keep the count. The blank, the order says twice, must never be cut a second time.
a3_hall: The door gallery is the last hundred yards, and it is lit: nine niches, nine lamps, all trimmed. The air moves in and out along the floor on a nine-count that everybody has been hearing all day without naming. Halfway along, a pair of Warden's boots stands neatly against the wall with the tags still in them.
a3_door: The Ninefold Door stands at the end of everything, dwarf iron set in a frame of much older stone, with nine sockets arranged in a ring. Eight of them are filled and warm. The ninth is empty and worn bright. The metal of the door moves very slightly outward and back on a nine-count, and behind it, patient and enormous, is something that is neither asleep nor awake.
e_a3_landing_rest: Twenty minutes on the first landing with boots off, which the keeper's board warned about in chalk in words of one syllable. The stair's own traffic arrives on schedule and finds a company sitting down in the middle of a right of way that has been in continuous use for nine hundred years.
e_a3_shrine_take: A token comes out of the second niche, and the seven remaining tokens all turn a quarter turn in their sockets at the same moment. The stair below fills with the sound of somebody coming up two flights at a time in order to correct an error in the arrangement.
e_a3_count_steps: The steps are counted aloud in the dark to keep five people together, which works admirably for the first eight numbers. At nine a second voice takes over the counting from somewhere below the company, and continues without any break in the rhythm. Everybody keeps descending, because the numbers keep arriving, and every single one of them is correct.
e_a3_grab: A hand goes out to take hold of what is passing on the stair, and it turns out to be entirely willing to be held. It has been waiting a considerable time for somebody to initiate the transaction rather than merely submit to it, and it is grateful in its own fashion.
e_a3_slack: The rope is hauled in hand over hand and comes up cut clean at forty feet, with no scout and no signal on the end of it. The company climbs four hundred steps back to a hillside in daylight, to compose a letter to a fen family about somebody who always went down first.
e_a3_shout: A hail goes down a dwarf hall in the correct Warden form, and the answer comes back accurately from six directions at once, in six voices the company heard reading a duty roster upstairs. The lamps out in the flooded gallery all turn together toward the foot of the stair.
e_a3_sink: The ferry is holed from underneath and goes down in eight feet of warm water with its crate still lashed amidships. The crate opens as it sinks, and whatever the Compact had packed into it decides, reasonably enough, that the nearest hands in the water will do perfectly well.
e_a3_swim: One breath taken, and one look down into warm black water with a lamp held under the surface to see by. The thing that has been turning over below the company for the whole crossing turns over once more, without any hurry at all, in order to look back up.
e_a3_ledge: The broken span of the ledge is taken as a shortcut, on the reasonable assumption that dwarf stone fails slowly and gives warning. It does fail slowly, everywhere except here, where nine hundred years of warm water have been working patiently at the mortar from underneath.
e_a3_crate: The bound Warden is asked what he is counting toward, and he answers in detail, with dates, in a voice that becomes several voices in the course of the reply. The lamps down the gallery stop their work in order to listen, and the company is still standing in the water when they finish.
e_a3_bell: The pay-bell is rung once in a deep hall, which is precisely what a pay-bell is for. The garrison answers it: eleven from behind the barracks barricade, the paymaster's clerks up out of the flooded gallery, and all of them forming into the old order to be paid what they are owed.
e_a3_hands: A search for a dead paymaster's hands succeeds. They are set in the wall's tally-groove where they have been cutting the same nine strokes over and over for eleven years, and they are still working when the lamp finds them, and they stop the moment they are noticed.
e_a3_eight_all: Eight key-irons come out of eight warm sockets in under a minute, taken by a company that came here for salvage and stayed for the arithmetic. The Ninefold Door then does exactly what nine hundred years of dwarf engineering, nine irons, and nine hands were arranged to prevent it from doing.
e_a3_read_end: The wall-tally is read down to the bottom of the final group, where the ninth stroke has been begun and then left unfinished halfway. Beside it a name has been cut into the stone in fresh, bright work that has not yet had time to dull. It is not the paymaster's name and it is not Coren Vale's name; it is the name of whoever happens to be reading it.
e_a3_burn_wall: A lamp breaks against nine hundred years of accounts and the chapel goes up in a light that shows exactly what is sitting on all nine benches. Vale stands in the middle of the fire entirely unharmed, apologising for the inconvenience, and explaining that the tally is not kept on the wall.
e_a3_accept: A name is spoken aloud in a warm chapel, and Vale writes it into his book without hurry and blots it carefully. The company walks out of the hill four strong and genuinely rich, with the frontier safe for nine more years, and that is a real thing that was really bought, and none of the four can look directly at it.
e_a3_accept_self: The captain's own name goes into the ninth hand's book, and the company is sent up the stair with the ledger, the iron, and the back pay. A new keeper sits down at a clerk's desk to learn a count that has been running for nine hundred years and shows no sign whatsoever of finishing.
e_a3_hostage: Coren Vale walks to the Ninefold Door at knifepoint as surety, entirely cooperative and faintly amused by the whole arrangement. On the way he explains, conversationally, that a hostage is only ever worth what the other party is unwilling to lose. The thing behind this door has never been unwilling to lose anything at all, and he has watched it prove that nine times.
e_a3_chapel_defends: A stand is made in a chapel against nine benches of standing dust, and the company wins it for something over ninety seconds. Then it loses, for the reason Vale did not think worth mentioning, which is that everybody who has ever sat down in that room remains on the roll.
e_a3_vale_count: The silence after Vale's death is waited out, to learn what a count does when it has no keeper. The answer arrives from the direction of the door within four minutes: it looks for the nearest hand that has held an iron today, and it is not remotely particular about consent.
e_a3_wheel: A ride down the wheel-race on a paddle, to establish where the water actually goes. It goes to a shaft, and then to a sump, and then into a chamber that the dwarves pumped out continuously for nine hundred years for a reason they wrote down in three separate places.
e_a3_pump_stay: The company stays at the pump, because the deep has to be kept dry and somebody has to do it. Shifts are worked on dwarf machinery for eleven days, and the door business is left for the Wardens, who arrive in spring and find a wheel in excellent order with nobody attending it.
e_a3_drown_own: The wheel jams on the captain's word with Kettle and Odd still on the low side of the race. Nine hundred years of held water goes precisely where it has always wanted to go, considerably faster than anybody can climb, and the shouting stops before the water does.
e_a3_race: The wheel-race is crossed together and quickly, because the Fenkin crew has seen you and is shouting, which puts two people in the gap at the same moment. The gap between two paddles has always been exactly one person wide, and the wheel does not adjust for enthusiasm.
e_a3_ring: A ring is taken off the arm of a chair that has no king sitting in it. All nine attendants turn their heads together to see who has accepted the office, and the plaque beneath the ninth chair turns out, on closer reading, to have been a job description all along.
e_a3_through: One long look at the occupied chair, taken deliberately, so that at least one person in the company would be able to say what was actually in the room. The thing in the chair returns the courtesy in full, and at considerable length, and by then nobody is leaving.
e_a3_forge_light: A dwarf forge is lit for the first time in nine hundred years, because the company wants heat and working light and both are reasonable. The flue runs, as dwarf flues do, straight up into the pay-hall and straight down into the door gallery, announcing the work to everything that has ever worked here.
e_a3_second: A second ninth iron is cut on a die whose own written orders state twice that the blank must never be cut a second time. In the space of one hammer stroke the hill's arithmetic acquires a tenth hand, for which it has no socket, no schedule, and no tolerance whatsoever.
e_a3_knock_door: Three knocks on the Ninefold Door, since knocking worked so well at the gate. The door answers them: three knocks returned from the other side in exactly the same rhythm, at a scale that brings dust off the ceiling and removes every opinion from everybody present in about two seconds.
e_a3_leave: Four hundred steps back up, out through the gap in the door, across the moor, and into Gallowmere by the second evening. The report says the vault is unsafe and says nothing else at all, and five people spend the remainder of their lives not talking about the same afternoon.
e_a3_tags: Two Warden tags are lifted out of a pair of boots that were set down neatly by their owner in a place where nothing at all is neat by accident. The nine lamps of the gallery go out in order from the far end, and the boots turn out, on reflection, to have been a place setting.
